overview:
Bhutan is a small kingdom folded into the eastern Himalayas, squeezed between two giants, China to the north and India to the south. It has no coastline and no flat land to speak of; even the lowest valleys sit hundreds of meters above the sea. At about 38,400 km² it is a little smaller than Switzerland, and fewer than 800,000 people live there.

The Bhutanese call their country Druk Yul, the Land of the Thunder Dragon, and a white dragon coils across the national flag. The capital, Thimphu, is one of the few capitals in the world without a single traffic light; a police officer in white gloves directs cars at the main crossroads. Dzongkha is the national language, and Buddhism shapes nearly every part of life.

Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. Instead of measuring success only by money, the government aims for Gross National Happiness, weighing health, culture and the environment. Farming, hydroelectric power sold to India, and carefully limited tourism support the economy.
landAndNature:
From subtropical jungles along the Indian border, the land climbs through pine and rhododendron forests to glaciers and peaks above 7,000 meters. Gangkhar Puensum, about 7,570 meters, is considered the highest mountain in the world that no one has climbed, because Bhutan forbids climbing its sacred summits. Rivers rush south through deep valleys, powering the country's dams.

The constitution requires that at least 60 percent of Bhutan stay forested, and more than 70 percent is. Those forests soak up more carbon dioxide than the country produces. Bengal tigers have been photographed above 4,000 meters, sharing the mountains with snow leopards, red pandas and the takin, a shaggy national animal that looks like a cross between a goat and a cow. Black-necked cranes fly in from Tibet each winter to the Phobjikha Valley.
peopleAndCulture:
Dzongkha is the national language, but about 20 other languages are spoken in the valleys, and English is used in schools. Most people are Buddhists, and prayer flags flutter from bridges and ridgelines. Men wear the gho, a knee-length robe, and women the kira, a long woven dress, to school, work and festivals.

The favorite dish is ema datshi, chilies cooked in melted cheese and eaten with red rice; Bhutanese treat chilies as a vegetable, not a spice. Archery is the national sport, played with loud teasing, singing and dancing between shots. Tshechu festivals fill fortress courtyards with masked dancers acting out Buddhist stories. Bhutan allowed television and the internet only in 1999, and it protects its culture carefully while young people also enjoy K-pop and soccer.
history:
People have farmed Bhutan's valleys for thousands of years, and Buddhism arrived from Tibet in the 600s and 700s, brought by teachers such as Guru Rinpoche, who is said to have flown to a cliff at Paro on the back of a tigress; the Tiger's Nest monastery clings there today. In the 1600s a Tibetan lama, Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, united the valleys and built the huge fortress-monasteries called dzongs that still serve as government offices.

Bhutan was never colonized, though it fought and then made treaties with British India. In 1907 Ugyen Wangchuck became the first hereditary king, founding the dynasty that still reigns. Later kings opened roads, schools and hospitals from the 1960s. The fourth king gave up much of his power, and in 2008 Bhutan held its first democratic elections and adopted a constitution.
funFacts: Bhutan is one of the few carbon-negative countries in the world; its forests absorb more carbon dioxide than its people produce.
Thimphu is one of the very few national capitals with no traffic lights; drivers follow the hand signals of police officers.
Climbing mountains above 6,000 meters is banned in Bhutan out of respect for the spirits believed to live there.
Bhutan banned plastic bags in 1999 and in 2004 became the first country to outlaw the sale of tobacco.
Many older Bhutanese celebrate their birthday on January 1, because exact birth dates were not recorded when they were born.
Bhutanese archers use bamboo bows and shoot at targets about 145 meters away, nearly twice the Olympic distance.
